title: Rocks, Lava and Mountains
subtitle: How the ground under you was made
subject: Earth

pages.h: The ground is a thin shell
p: The ground feels solid and still. But Earth is like a giant egg. The hard crust you stand on is the shell. It is only about 5 to 70 kilometres thick.

Under the crust is the mantle, a thick layer of very hot rock that moves slowly, like thick honey. In the middle is the core, a ball of iron. The centre is about 5,000 degrees Celsius, nearly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
pages.cap: Crust, mantle, core. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets.
pages.fact: Did you know? The deepest hole people have ever drilled is 12 kilometres. That is not even through the crust.

p: Deep under some places, rock gets so hot that it melts. Melted rock underground is called magma. It is lighter than the rock around it, so it rises.
When it finds a crack to the surface, it bursts out. Now it is called lava. Lava can be more than 1,000 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt a pop can. A mountain built by lava is a volcano.
pages.cap: Magma rises, then pours out as lava. Ash and gas blast into the sky.
pages.fact: Did you know? Lava is so hot that it glows orange, like a stove turned up to full.

p: Earth's crust is broken into huge pieces called plates. They fit together like a cracked eggshell and move a few centimetres each year.

Most volcanoes sit where two plates meet. Around the edge of the Pacific Ocean, so many volcanoes line up that it is called the Ring of Fire. Earth has about 1,350 volcanoes that could still erupt. About 50 of them erupt each year.
pages.cap: Where plates push together, one slides under the other and the rock melts.
pages.fact: Did you know? Canada has volcanoes too. Most are in British Columbia, and one erupted only a few hundred years ago.

pages.q: What is melted rock called once it comes out of a volcano?
pages.why: Underground it is magma. Once it flows out onto the surface, it is called lava.

pages.h: The day the sky went dark
p: In the year 79, in Italy, a volcano called Vesuvius exploded. Ash and hot gas buried the town of Pompeii under 6 metres of grey ash. The town stayed hidden for almost 1,700 years.
In 1815, Tambora in Indonesia blew up so hard that its ash cooled the whole world. The next year, snow fell in June in parts of Canada and the United States.
pages.fact: Did you know? In 2022, the Hunga Tonga volcano shot ash 57 kilometres high, far above where planes fly.

pages.h: The tallest volcano is on Mars
p: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 kilometres high. That is two and a half times taller than Mount Everest. It is so wide that if you stood on its slope, you would not even see it as a mountain.
In 1963, fishermen near Iceland saw smoke rising from the sea. A volcano was erupting under the water. Within days, a brand-new island rose up. It is called Surtsey.

Every island of Hawaii was built this way, layer by layer, from lava. The biggest one is still growing. One Hawaiian volcano, Mauna Kea, is over 10,000 metres from its base on the sea floor to its top. Measured that way, it is taller than Everest.
pages.cap: Lava flows into the sea, cools, and the island grows.
pages.fact: Did you know? Iceland is still growing. It gains about 2 centimetres a year as plates pull apart under it.

p: Make your own eruption.
steps: Stand a small cup in a tray. Pile sand or play dough around it to make a mountain.
Put 2 spoons of baking soda in the cup. Add a squirt of dish soap and a few drops of red food colouring.
Pour in half a cup of vinegar. Stand back!
Watch the foam flow down the sides, just like lava.
Try more soda or more vinegar. Which makes a bigger eruption?
pages.cap: Gas bubbles push the foam up and out. Real volcanoes have gas inside too.
pages.safe: Do this outside or in a tray. Keep vinegar out of your eyes.

p: When lava cools, it turns hard. The rock it makes is called igneous rock, which means rock from fire.

If lava cools fast in the air or water, the rock is smooth or full of holes. Pumice has so many gas holes that it floats. Obsidian cools so fast it becomes black glass. If magma cools slowly underground, over thousands of years, big crystals grow. That makes granite, with its sparkly speckles.
pages.cap: Hot and runny becomes cold and hard. Lava freezes into rock.
pages.fact: Did you know? Obsidian can be chipped to an edge sharper than a steel knife.

pages.q: What does a volcano need to build a new island?
opts: Lots of lava cooling and piling up
Lots of sand blown by wind
pages.why: Lava flows out, cools into hard rock and piles up, layer by layer, until it rises above the sea.

p: Rivers carry sand, mud and tiny shells to the sea. They settle on the bottom in a thin layer. The next year, another layer lands on top. And another.

After millions of years, the layers are squeezed so hard by their own weight that they turn to stone. This is sedimentary rock. Sandstone is old sand. Limestone is old sea shells. The Grand Canyon's stripes are these layers.
pages.cap: Layer on layer. The bottom ones are the oldest.
pages.fact: Did you know? Chalk is made of the shells of sea creatures so small you need a microscope to see them.

p: Sometimes a dead animal or plant gets buried in mud before it rots. Over millions of years, the mud turns to rock and the bones turn to stone. That is a fossil.
Because new layers go on top of old ones, the deepest fossils are the oldest. Reading the layers is like reading a book from the bottom up. Each page is a chapter of Earth's story.
pages.fact: Did you know? Fossils of sea shells have been found near the top of Mount Everest. That rock was once a sea floor.

p: In Alberta, Canada, there is a place called the Badlands where dinosaur bones stick out of the hills. More than 50 kinds of dinosaur have been found there.

One of the biggest dinosaurs ever found was Patagotitan, dug up in Argentina. It was about 37 metres long, longer than a basketball court, and may have weighed 60 tonnes. All we know about it comes from bones turned to rock.
pages.cap: A long-necked giant walks. Its bones may become fossils one day.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Royal Tyrrell Museum in Alberta holds more than 160,000 fossils.

p: Near Yellowknife in Canada's Northwest Territories, there is rock that is 4 billion years old. It formed before the first living thing. It is one of the oldest rocks ever found on Earth.

pages.q: Where are the oldest fossils in a cliff of rock layers?
pages.why: New layers land on top of old ones, so the deepest layers and their fossils are the oldest.

p: Deep underground, rock gets squeezed by the weight above it and heated by the hot mantle below. It does not melt. It changes.

This is metamorphic rock, which means changed rock. Soft limestone becomes hard, shiny marble. Mud rock becomes slate, which splits into flat sheets for roofs. The squeeze down there can be 10,000 times the air pressure you feel right now.
pages.cap: Heat and squeezing can change one kind of rock into another.
pages.fact: Did you know? Diamonds form about 150 kilometres down, where the squeeze is huge, and ride up to the surface inside volcanoes.

p: Rocks seem like the most permanent things in the world. They are not. They are always changing, just very slowly.

A mountain wears down into sand. The sand turns into sandstone. The sandstone gets buried and cooked into harder rock. That rock melts into magma, and bursts out as lava to make new rock. Then it starts all over again. Scientists call this the rock cycle.
pages.cap: Water goes round and round. Rocks go round too, but one trip can take millions of years.
pages.fact: Did you know? A grain of sand on a beach might once have been part of a mountain, a sea floor and a volcano.

p: About 50 million years ago, India crashed slowly into Asia. The crust crumpled up like a rug pushed against a wall. The crumples are the Himalayas.
India is still pushing. Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth, grows about 4 millimetres every year. The Rocky Mountains in Canada were pushed up the same way, by plates squeezing together.
pages.cap: Two plates push together and the ground folds up into mountains.
pages.fact: Did you know? Everest is 8,849 metres tall. Airliners fly only a little higher than its top.

pages.h: Try it: layers in a jar
p: Make your own rock layers.
steps: Find a clear jar with a lid.
Add a handful each of gravel, sand and garden soil.
Fill the jar with water, close the lid tight, and shake hard for 30 seconds.
Set it down and wait an hour. Watch the layers settle: heavy gravel first, then sand, then fine mud on top.
Leave it a day. Draw the layers. Real rock layers form the same way, but take millions of years.
pages.cap: Heavy bits sink first. Light mud settles last.
pages.safe: Use a plastic jar if you can, and clean up any spills.

p: Nothing lasts forever, not even a mountain. Rain washes grit off the top. Ice freezes in cracks and splits rock apart. Rivers cut valleys. Wind sandblasts cliffs.

The Appalachian Mountains in eastern North America were once as tall as the Himalayas. Hundreds of millions of years of rain and ice have worn them down to gentle hills. The sand on your beach may be old mountain.
pages.cap: Loose rock tumbles downhill. Rivers carry the bits to the sea.
pages.fact: Did you know? Niagara Falls has worn its way about 11 kilometres upriver in the last 12,000 years.

pages.q: What makes a mountain grow taller?
pages.why: When plates squeeze together, the crust crumples and folds upward. That is how the Himalayas and Rockies rose.

p: Plates do not slide smoothly. They stick, then suddenly jerk free. The jerk sends waves through the ground. That is an earthquake.

Most earthquakes are too small to feel. Canada records about 4,000 every year, mostly in British Columbia. Big ones can crack roads and shake buildings. In earthquake country, tall buildings are built to bend and sway instead of break.
pages.cap: Tall buildings in earthquake zones often sit on rubber pads that soak up the shaking.
pages.fact: Did you know? Japan gets about 1,500 earthquakes a year that people can feel.

p: Not every rock on Earth was made here. Every day, about 50 tonnes of space dust and tiny rocks fall onto our planet. Most burn up as shooting stars.
Some are big enough to land. These are meteorites. The biggest one ever found, in Namibia, weighs about 60 tonnes. Most meteorites are grey or black with a thin burnt crust. Some are solid iron.
pages.cap: A streak of light in the night sky is a rock from space burning up.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Tagish Lake meteorite fell on a frozen lake in northern British Columbia in 2000. Pieces were picked up from the ice a week later.

p: Rocks are not just outside. They are in your house and your pocket. The salt on your chips was dug from rock. The grey tip of a pencil is a rock called graphite.
Glass is melted sand. Coins are metals melted out of rock. A phone has more than 30 different metals in it, from mines all over the world. Even the bricks in a wall are baked clay from the ground.
pages.cap: Canadian coins are made mostly from steel and nickel, both dug out of rock.
pages.fact: Did you know? A Canadian nickel is mostly steel, with a thin coat of nickel on top.

p: Volcanoes sound like trouble, but they help us too. Volcanic ash is full of the minerals plants need. Farms around volcanoes grow some of the richest crops in the world.
In Iceland, hot rock underground heats most homes. The water comes out of the ground already hot. Long ago, volcanoes breathed out the gases that became Earth's air and oceans. No volcanoes, no us.
pages.cap: Ash makes rich soil, and seeds grow strong in it.
pages.fact: Did you know? Around 800 million people live within 100 kilometres of a volcano that could erupt.
